testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee and restriction policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Removing restrictions from Five Civilized Tribes Indians
testimony.key_claims: Would be governed by value of land in deciding whether to sell. Poor rough land worth only a couple dollars an acre not worth selling in small tracts. In some cases would remove restrictions and let Indian sell with understanding that if he makes good and invests properly, restrictions would be removed from other land later. Old and feeble Indians with no money to live on should be allowed to sell land a piece at a time. Believes 80 percent of Indians have wasted all property given them. Removal of all restrictions would mean great poverty. Has not met a white man who would not like to see restrictions removed - they are jealous of Indians and want them to pay taxes and work roads.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee and restriction policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Turning Indians loose without Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Turning Indians loose without supervision would be a sad mistake. There is always some grafter ready to buy, borrow, beg or steal whatever the Indian has privilege to sell. It would be all right if all men were honest but people think it is not wrong to cheat the Indian. Five Civilized Tribes would be better off financially if there never had been any restrictions removed. Knows several cases where restrictions were removed and Indians have nothing to show for proceeds. However in another way believes it made better citizens out of some Indians - once they sold and became broke, some thought themselves too good to work but then found honest labor. Knows some who sold allotments who now depend entirely on labor for living. Indians of Five Civilized Tribes have full citizenship in regard to voting and holding office. As fast as restricted Indians prove themselves competent they should be turned loose. Worst enemy is whiskey, corn whiskey, Jake, and various intoxicants and dope.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Omak, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Success or failure of patent-in-fee policy at Colville
testimony.key_claims: Economic or financial competency is not a tangible possession like education or degree of blood. Majority of Indians and majority of white people do not have excessive acquisitiveness - most wealth is in hands of small percentage. Believes in liberal policy on patent-in-fee issuance. When an Indian desires a patent it argues financial incompetence or that economic disadvantage of paying taxes outweighs benefit of land ownership dignity. Six cases out of ten the actual reason for requesting patent is to get control of land to secure money by sale or mortgage. Policy of wholesale patent issuance serves as education to entire tribe about risk of losing allotments. Negative examples are more noticeable than positive steady-going Indians who retain land. Submitted reports of three district farmers.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Inchelium, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Benefits or disadvantages of fee patents in Inchelium district
testimony.key_claims: District has larger percentage of mixed-blood Indians. Degree of blood has very little influence on whether patent was beneficial. Full-bloods have made good after patent and some with very little Indian blood have dissipated allotments. Majority of cases where patents issued have been beneficial or at least not detrimental. All adult competent Indians in district have already received patents. Some competent Indians do not desire patents because of added tax burden. Best to examine each individual case on its merits, with field employee's judgment as basis. Names Theodore Bourgeau, Victor Dupuie, Barney Richard, Peter Noyes, Nancy Moore, D.L. Skeels as successful cases. Names Willie Ferguson, Marcelle Lafleur, Henry Stensgar, Joseph Noel as detrimental cases. Joseph Mullen a nuanced case - sold allotment but improved other land.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Nespelem, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians in Nespelem district
testimony.key_claims: Of 17 Indians in Nespelem district, 11 have sold their allotments and only 3 have anything of value to show for the money. In some cases disposition was justified because lands were not agricultural and could not furnish a living. Describes Charley Bob farming father's and deceased mother's allotments, built house/barn/fence/alfalfa, in heavy debt, original allotment only grazing land worth about $1,000. Ross Hilleary sold allotment, borders McGinnis Lake, now used for irrigation with 80 tillable acres, bought a car. Tom Andrews traded part of allotment for Ford car, owes Government $644.88. Sam Friedlander sold allotment to brother's wife for $2500. William Friedlander still on allotment with 100 acres cultivation, sold 25 cattle and used proceeds to improve allotment. Paul Smitakin farming father's allotment, working as forest guard, plans business college. Charley Hilburn traded allotment for King Eight car, good mechanic but not energetic. Hiram Runnels sold north half of allotment, now on child's allotment, awaiting appointment to US Dry Squad. Arcasa boys sold grazing land allotments, well educated and employed. Bill Condon competent, holds and leases allotment, successful stock raiser. Dan Condon sold allotment for about $2,000, now in stock raising. Whitelaw brothers John, Pete and George successful in farming and stock raising, accumulated 100 head of cattle. Pakatas boys Mose and Philip each sold allotments for $10,000, money going fast.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Fort Peck Agency, Poplar, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee Indians at Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Patents-in-fee have been issued to Indians without enough thought about future conditions. Most patent-in-fee Indians he knows have failed. About 50 percent who received patents after board review are making good, retaining land, stock, implements and homes. Most patent-in-fee Indians sold land and first bought automobile, then some farm machinery and stock. When cash ran out they sold stock and machinery, last the automobile. Indians on reservation have been allotted only a short time and for several years after allotments no land was leased or income received. Not expected that in short time people would know how to handle land or money. Indians had no responsibility or business training. No patent should be given to entire allotment - homestead of 30 to 40 acres should be held in trust indefinitely. Patents should not be issued without application being passed on by competent board that has known applicant for at least several years. Superintendent fell in with Office desire to issue patents profusely as matter of loyalty. Some Indians objected to citizenship because they desired to keep property exempt from taxation. Others dissatisfied because they have lost their heritage. Bad practice of living off children's money should be prohibited except in very extreme cases. Names specific successful cases: William Manning, David Manning, Francis and Alfred Murray, Charles Seeds, Daniel Courchene, Fred Bauer, Traffle Sears. Names failed cases: Joe Alvarez, John Anderson, John Bruguior, William Boyd.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Box Elder Sub-agency, Brockton, Montana, Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Conditions of patent-in-fee Indians on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Issuance of fee patents to Indians declared as citizens with expectation of making them self-supporting has been a failure to a large extent on this reservation. Conditions were far better for Indians before they were given citizenship because of Government control and protection from land selling. Almost without exception, Indians made citizens and given patent to all their land are selling allotments outright or mortgaging them for part cash and an automobile. Indians use automobiles for joy rides until all spent, then lose land. Pattern of coming back to superintendent to request patents on additional allotments after first is lost. Conditions for past several years in this vicinity have been bad for 90 percent of white people too. In future patents should not be issued so freely - more careful examination of character needed and homestead should be retained. Cites specific cases including John Bruguior addicted to drink, dissipated everything. Present practice of issuing patents is most too liberal.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on restriction policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Advisability of removing all restrictions from Indians and letting them have their property
testimony.key_claims: In reply to letter of 5th inst. inquiring about removing all restrictions. 80 percent of Indians have wasted all that was given to them and have nothing to show. Indians do not live right, are easily influenced. People associating with them do not set good example, tell them Indian Service people just have easy jobs and are doing the skinning. Some people do all they can to influence Indians against Indian Service employees and their advice. Business men quite often advise Indians to make bad investments when it benefits white men. It would be all right if all men would tell the truth, but most people think it is not wrong to cheat the Indian.
